answer.label: Not Maslow's words — a smoothed paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, founder of humanistic psychology
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Maslow’s, but this is not how he put it. In The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (Viking, 1971), in chapter 2 — “Neurosis as a Failure of Personal Growth,” pp. 33–35, where he introduces the Jonah complex — the sentence is reported as “If you deliberately plan to be less than you are capable of being, then I warn you that you’ll be deeply unhappy for the rest of your life.” The tidier “plan on being anything less … unhappy all the days of your life” version is a later rewrite: Wikiquote files it under Attributed, and the only citation it can offer is a 2004 self-help book.

source.excerpt: If you deliberately plan to be less than you are capable of being, then I warn you that you’ll be deeply unhappy for the rest of your life. You will be evading your own capacities, your own possibilities.
trail: Wikiquote does not put this sentence among Maslow’s sourced quotations at all — it sits in the Attributed section, cited to Joan Neehall-Davidson’s Perfecting Private Practice (2004), p. 95 (Wikiquote ↗).

The wording Maslow is actually recorded as using belongs to chapter 2 of The Farther Reaches of Human Nature — “Neurosis as a Failure of Personal Growth,” pp. 33–35, where the Jonah complex is introduced. The sentence itself is quoted verbatim, and credited to that book, by Academy of Ideas ↗; a counselling study resource transcribes the surrounding passage and cites the same pages (PDF ↗), though its transcription stops at the classroom question and does not carry the warning.
The book itself is catalogued as New York: Viking Press, 1971 — published after Maslow’s death in June 1970 (Internet Archive record ↗).
Independent writing on the Jonah complex quotes the “deliberately plan” wording verbatim and credits it to that book, never to the smoothed version (Academy of Ideas ↗).
source.excerptNote: These sentences follow the classroom question — “Which of you in this class hopes to write the great American novel, or to be a Senator, or Governor, or President?” — which appears in exactly that form in the Internet Archive’s full-text index of the 1971 Viking scan; the Counselling Study Resource ↗ transcribes the same passage from pp. 33–34, lowercasing the offices. The scan itself is lending-restricted, so the excerpt above is taken from sources that quote and cite the book rather than read off the page — and an exact-phrase search of that index does not return the warning sentence, which may reflect the printed wording or simply OCR and line breaks.

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.heading: About Abraham Maslow
author.metaLine: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, founder of humanistic psychology
author.bio: Abraham Maslow was an American psychologist who taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University and gave the world the hierarchy of needs and popularized the term self-actualization, which he took from Kurt Goldstein and credited to him. He spent his last decade arguing that psychology had studied damage far more carefully than it had studied flourishing, and that most people quietly settle for less than they could be. He died in June 1970; The Farther Reaches of Human Nature, the collection that carries this passage, appeared in 1971.

misattribution.heading: How the wording drifted
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from another author — the thinking is unmistakably Maslow’s. What is wrong is the sentence itself, and the confident way it is presented as a direct quotation.

items.why: Wikiquote lists “If you plan on being anything less than you are capable of being, you will probably be unhappy all the days of your life” in its Attributed section, and the only citation it offers is Joan Neehall-Davidson, Perfecting Private Practice (2004), p. 95 — a book published thirty-odd years after Maslow’s death, not anything he wrote (Wikiquote ↗).
Goodreads and its imitators print the smoothed version with no book, no chapter and no page — Goodreads’ own page carries the notice that quotes are added by users and are not verified (Goodreads ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: What Maslow is recorded as writing, in chapter 2 of The Farther Reaches of Human Nature — “Neurosis as a Failure of Personal Growth,” where the Jonah complex is introduced — is sharper: a personal warning about deliberately planning to be less, and about evading your own capacities (wording quoted verbatim and credited to the book ↗).

context.heading: The classroom question behind it
lead: Maslow called it the Jonah complex — after the prophet who ran from what he was called to do — and he had a party trick for demonstrating it. He would ask a lecture room, in the wording the book’s own scan preserves, “Which of you in this class hopes to write the great American novel, or to be a Senator, or Governor, or President?” The room would squirm. That squirm, he argued, was the whole problem: we are frightened of our best possibilities, not only our worst (Counselling Study Resource ↗).

The warning that follows is the sentence the internet remembers — badly. Maslow wrote it as a warning delivered in the second person, hedge-free: deliberately plan to be less, and you will be deeply unhappy for the rest of your life, evading your own capacities. Somewhere between the 1971 book and the poster industry it was sanded down into something gentler and more quotable, and it is the sanded version that now circulates under his name.
context.detailsSummary: What actually changed in the rewrite
detailsBody: Two changes every rendering of Maslow’s sentence agrees on. Then I warn you that you’ll be deeply unhappy — a direct, personal warning — becomes the hedged you will probably be unhappy. And for the rest of your life becomes the biblical-sounding all the days of your life. A third change is real but harder to pin down: Maslow’s opening carries deliberately, which the popular version drops altogether — though the sources we could check disagree over whether he wrote deliberately plan to be less or deliberately plan on being less, and we have not read the printed page.
None of that makes the sentiment un-Maslovian; it makes the sentence a paraphrase. If you need to quote him, quote the version that is actually in the book — and cite the book.
context.pull: Maslow’s own label for it was blunter: “fear of one’s own greatness.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "If you plan on being anything less than you are capable of being, you will probably be unhappy all the days of your life" in its Attributed section, citing Joan Neehall-Davidson, Perfecting Private Practice (2004), p. 95.
The Farther Reaches of Human Nature by Abraham H. Maslow is catalogued as New York: Viking Press, 1971.

The passage including "Which of you in this class hopes to write the great American novel, or to be a Senator, or Governor, or President?" is transcribed from Maslow's essay "The Jonah Complex" in The Farther Reaches of Human Nature, and Maslow's own label for the defence was "fear of one's own greatness".

The wording "If you deliberately plan to be less than you are capable of being, then I warn you that you'll be deeply unhappy for the rest of your life" is quoted verbatim and attributed to The Farther Reaches of Human Nature.
The same 'deliberately plan' wording, with the continuation "You will be evading your own capacities, your own possibilities", is cited to The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971).
Goodreads shows the popular wording credited to Abraham Maslow with no book or source citation, and notes that quotes are community-added and not verified.

Abraham Maslow lived 1 April 1908 to 8 June 1970 and was an American psychologist who created the hierarchy of needs and founded humanistic psychology, teaching at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University.
ERIC document ED012056 is the full text of Maslow's 1965 address "Self-Actualization and Beyond"; the quoted sentence does not appear in it.
Open Library's search-inside returns The Farther Reaches of Human Nature among books literally containing "or to be a Senator, or Governor, or President? Who wants to be Secretary-General...".
